reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Endocrine Society clinical guidance
clinicalPearls: A congenital deficiency of gonadotropin-releasing hormone secretion or action, with an intact sense of smell, distinguishing it from Kallmann syndrome
Presents with absent or arrested puberty and low sex steroids in the face of low or inappropriately normal gonadotropins
Males may show micropenis and cryptorchidism reflecting deficient fetal and neonatal gonadotropin exposure
A eunuchoid body habitus with a long arm span develops when hypogonadism goes untreated through adolescence
Implicated genes include GNRHR, GNRH1, KISS1R, TAC3 and TACR3, affecting the GnRH neuroendocrine axis without olfactory involvement
A minority of patients show reversal of the condition after a period of treatment, so the axis should be periodically reassessed
Treatment goals are sex-steroid replacement to induce and maintain secondary sexual characteristics, with gonadotropin or pulsatile GnRH therapy when fertility is desired
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism results from defective secretion or action of hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone, which normally drives pituitary secretion of luteinising hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone. In the normosmic form the GnRH neurons migrate and the olfactory system develops normally, but signalling defects (for example in the GnRH receptor, kisspeptin or neurokinin B pathways) blunt pulsatile GnRH output. Reduced gonadotropin drive leaves the gonads understimulated, so sex-steroid production and gametogenesis fail and puberty does not proceed. The deficiency of sex steroids also removes the signal for epiphyseal fusion, producing the characteristic eunuchoid proportions when untreated.
additionalDifferentials: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
Functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (chronic illness, excessive exercise, undernutrition)
Combined pituitary hormone deficiency or a hypothalamic-pituitary mass
additionalInvestigations: Basal luteinising hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone and sex steroids showing low gonadotropins with low sex hormones
Formal olfactory testing to confirm a normal sense of smell
Prolactin, thyroid and other pituitary hormone assessment to exclude broader hypopituitarism
Pituitary MRI to exclude a structural lesion
Genetic testing of GnRH-axis genes such as GNRHR, KISS1R and TACR3
Bone age and bone mineral density assessment
redFlags: Visual field defect, headache or other pituitary hormone deficits suggesting a sellar mass
Micropenis or cryptorchidism in an infant prompting early evaluation
Severely reduced bone density from prolonged sex-steroid deficiency
Features suggesting a syndromic or life-limiting associated condition
reference.prognosis: With appropriate hormone replacement, secondary sexual characteristics and bone health can be established and maintained, and fertility is often achievable with gonadotropin or pulsatile GnRH therapy. A subset experience spontaneous reversal, warranting periodic reassessment off treatment.
pitfalls: Confusing the condition with constitutional pubertal delay, which resolves spontaneously
Omitting olfactory testing and mislabelling it as Kallmann syndrome or vice versa
Failing to exclude a hypothalamic-pituitary tumour or hyperprolactinaemia
Assuming lifelong deficiency and not reassessing for reversal
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance on hypogonadism
